title: Are the survivors next in line?
hook: Half the atoms have decayed. Are the ones still here overdue?

knows: that matter is made of atoms
doesNotKnow: that decay is a random process for each nucleus

misconception: Atoms age like a timer: the ones that survive are 'overdue' (or 'tougher'), and the half that remains after one half-life is a predictable, special set. A common corollary is that two half-lives leave nothing.
objective: The learner can explain that every undecayed atom of an isotope has the same 50% chance of decaying in the next half-life, however long it has already lasted, so which atoms survive is random and survivors keep halving instead of running out.

claims.text: Radioactive decay is random for each nucleus: you can say how likely an atom is to decay, not when or which atom goes next.
claims.source: K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988), ch. 6.1: decay is a statistical process with a constant probability per unit time for each nucleus.

claims.text: In one half-life, each undecayed atom has a 50% chance of decaying, no matter how long it has already survived.
claims.source: Exponential decay N(t) = N0 * 2^(-t/T) implies a constant per-atom decay probability (memoryless). Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics, ch. 6.1; Rutherford & Soddy, Phil. Mag. 5 (1903) 576.

claims.text: After 2 half-lives about a quarter of the atoms remain, and after 3 about an eighth: survivors keep halving instead of running out.
With only a few hundred atoms, the share that decays in a half-life wanders around 50% by chance; with the trillions in a real sample it is extremely close to 50%.
claims.source: Each atom decays independently with p = 0.5 per half-life, so the count is binomial with standard deviation sqrt(n p (1-p)); relative spread shrinks as 1/sqrt(n). Simulated in the lesson with a seeded generator.

claims.text: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,700 years.
claims.source: NNDC/ENSDF evaluated value 5,700 +/- 30 years (Kondev et al., Chinese Physics C 45 (2021) 030001, NUBASE2020); the Cambridge value 5,730 +/- 40 years (Godwin, Nature 195 (1962) 984).

recall.question: One atom in a sample has already lasted 5 half-lives. Its chance of decaying during the next half-life is...
options: 50%, the same as any atom of that isotope
Less than 50%: it has proven stable
recall.why: Atoms do not age. Every undecayed atom has the same 50% chance per half-life, however long it has lasted.
